newsitem.title: CHINA: HK govt regrets Internet blunder with private data.
newsitem.headline: HK govt regrets Internet blunder with private data.

text.p: The Hong Kong government apologised on Thursday for an embarrassing blunder after accidentally posting the personal identity document numbers of hundreds of journalists on the Internet.

Local newspapers were fast to spot the government had posted a list of almost 1,000 journalists covering Monday night's Hong Kong handover to China on a WorldWide Web site, plus passport and identity card details, compromising their privacy.
Personal data of this kind is protected by Hong Kong's recently enacted privacy laws and enforcement is overseen by an independent watchdog body, the Privacy Commission.

The release of the data was an accident, Mary Leung, Chief Information Officer of the Government Information Services, who was in charge of press arrangements for the arrival of the People's Liberation Army on Monday and Tuesday, told Reuters.
"We required the journalists to register to attend the PLA troops' arrival, but our event was not limited to journalists, anyone could apply to attend it.
"The border is a restricted area so we need their ID and passport numbers to make border permits for them," Leung said.
She said the government originally had no intention of issuing a list but journalists wanted the government to release one to show whether their applications had been successful.
The government released the list at June 29, two days after it had sent out invitations to the press.
Leung said the information team looking after the media at the event had very little time to work out the logistics.

"Liaison with departments concerned, press registration and border permits and transport etcetera, had all to be done within 72 hours before the arrival of the first batch of PLA personnel at nine o'clock on the night of June 30," she said.
She said her staff worked overnight under extremely heavy pressure to process around 1,000 applications and the mistake was made because of exhaustion.
The name list was posted on the Internet on June 29 because of a technical oversight, and was removed by the government on July 2 after the mishap was spotted.
Leung believes the list might not have been much visited by net surfers, although the government's web site is open to everyone.
Apologising for the error, she said she believed it was an isolated incident that would not affect people's confidence in the protection of their personal information.
A spokesman for the Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal told Reuters all organisations had to respect the privacy laws, and confirmed the government's slip-up was a breach of privacy.
"If the government wants to show the journalists' names allocated to the place to cover a certain event, it's enough to show just the names of the news organisations and journalists.
"The ID and passports numbers were not necessary to be shown as well for this purpose." she said according to what she knew about the incident from a local newspaper.
"I welcome the government's remedial action...I don't think the public will lose confidence in the protection of personal information by the effect of just an insolated incident."
